source_note: Hand-written reference notes with a source link and an as-of date on every entry, resolved through Wikidata for identifiers and articles; images are Wikimedia Commons files with their licence and credit. Background, not intelligence.

equipment.name: Orlan-10
equipment.role: Tactical reconnaissance and artillery spotting drone
equipment.description: Russia's workhorse reconnaissance drone since 2014: a catapult-launched, petrol-engined aircraft flying for many hours with a camera turret, used to find targets for artillery and to relay corrections. Cheap enough to lose in numbers, and lost in numbers; its imported electronics have appeared in sanctions reporting.
equipment.numbers: Oryx has documented well over a thousand Orlan-10 and Orlan-30 losses since 2022 (visually confirmed, an undercount by design).

equipment.name: ZALA 421-16E
equipment.role: Reconnaissance drone from the Lancet's maker
equipment.description: A flying-wing reconnaissance drone from the ZALA Aero group of Kalashnikov Concern, normally paired with Lancet loitering munitions: the ZALA finds the target and the Lancet strikes it. Its long endurance and quiet electric motor make it hard to spot from the ground.

equipment.name: Supercam S350
equipment.role: Medium reconnaissance drone
equipment.description: A series of catapult-launched reconnaissance drones built by Unmanned Systems Group in Izhevsk, flown for artillery reconnaissance and for cueing strikes behind the line. Reported to be one of the more common Russian types seen over Ukrainian positions from 2023.

equipment.name: Leleka-100
equipment.role: Reconnaissance drone in Ukrainian service
equipment.description: A Ukrainian-built electric reconnaissance drone from DeViRo, adopted by the armed forces in 2021 and produced in growing numbers since. It spots for artillery and drone strikes and is one of several domestic types, with Shark and Furia, that replaced imported quadcopters for deeper reconnaissance.

equipment.name: Shark
equipment.role: Reconnaissance drone for HIMARS and artillery targeting
equipment.description: Ukrspecsystems' Shark reconnaissance drone entered service in 2022 and is often cited with long-range strikes, spotting for HIMARS and guided artillery at ranges of tens of kilometres. Ukraine has produced later variants with better resistance to jamming.

equipment.name: FPV strike drones (Russia)
equipment.role: First-person-view quadcopters carrying a warhead
equipment.description: Cheap racing-style quadcopters flown through goggles into vehicles, positions and individual soldiers, now the main killer on the front line for both sides. Russia scaled production through 2023 and 2024 with volunteer workshops and state-backed factories, and both sides count monthly deliveries in the hundreds of thousands.
equipment.numbers: Both governments have stated production plans in the millions per year; no independent count exists.

equipment.name: FPV strike drones (Ukraine)
equipment.role: First-person-view quadcopters carrying a warhead
equipment.description: Ukraine's FPV programme grew from volunteer builds in 2022 to hundreds of manufacturers and a dedicated Unmanned Systems Forces branch in 2024. FPVs with RPG warheads or shaped charges account for a large share of reported Russian vehicle losses, and strike units publish confirmed hits through a points-based system.
equipment.numbers: Ukraine's government stated a goal of several million FPV drones for 2025; no independent count exists.

equipment.name: Fibre-optic FPV drones (Russia)
equipment.role: Jam-proof FPV controlled through a spooled fibre
equipment.description: From late 2024 Russia fielded FPV drones controlled through a thin optical fibre unspooled in flight, immune to radio jamming and able to fly into cellars and treelines. They were prominent in the Kursk fighting and along the Pokrovsk axis, at the cost of shorter range and fibres snagging on terrain.

equipment.name: Fibre-optic FPV drones (Ukraine)
equipment.role: Jam-proof FPV controlled through a spooled fibre
equipment.description: Ukraine followed Russia's fibre-optic drones within months, with domestic spools of 10 to 20 kilometres and longer announced during 2025. Units use them where electronic warfare is dense, accepting the weight of the spool for a link that cannot be jammed.

equipment.name: ZALA Lancet
equipment.role: Loitering munition against artillery, air defence and armour
equipment.description: A tube-shaped loitering munition with cruciform wings that dives onto a target seen through its own camera, often cued by a ZALA reconnaissance drone. From 2023 it became Russia's most effective weapon against Ukrainian howitzers and air defence radars behind the line, and later versions added automatic target recognition.
equipment.numbers: Open-source trackers count thousands of published Lancet strike videos; the share that hit is disputed.

equipment.name: ZALA KUB
equipment.role: Flying-wing loitering munition
equipment.description: A small flying-wing loitering munition from the same maker as the Lancet, used from the first weeks of the invasion against fixed positions. It lacks the Lancet's precision against moving targets and appears less often in strike footage.

equipment.name: Switchblade 300 and 600
equipment.role: US loitering munitions supplied in aid packages
equipment.description: The Switchblade 300 is a small, short-range munition against infantry; the 600 carries an anti-armour warhead over longer range. Supplied from 2022, they mattered early but were overtaken by Ukraine's cheaper domestic FPV drones, which are produced in far greater numbers.
equipment.numbers: US aid announcements listed several hundred Switchblade 300s in 2022 and later Switchblade 600s.

equipment.name: Shahed-136 / Geran-2
equipment.role: Long-range one-way attack drone against cities and energy
equipment.description: A delta-wing drone with a petrol engine and a warhead of around 50 kilograms, first used by Russia in September 2022 and built since 2023 at Alabuga in Tatarstan as the Geran-2. Launched in waves of hundreds with decoys to saturate air defence, it is the main weapon of the strike campaign against Ukrainian cities and the power grid. Later versions add jet engines, larger warheads and jam-resistant navigation.
equipment.numbers: Ukraine's Air Force reported record nights of over 700 drones and decoys in 2025; the General Staff's cumulative drone claim is shown in the figures above.

equipment.name: Geran-3 (jet Shahed)
equipment.role: Jet-powered one-way attack drone
equipment.description: A jet-engined development of the Shahed family, faster and harder for mobile fire groups to catch, used in growing numbers from 2025 inside the larger propeller-driven waves. Its speed cuts the time air defence has to react.

equipment.name: An-196 Liutyi
equipment.role: Long-range one-way attack drone against Russian refineries and airfields
equipment.description: A Ukrainian-built one-way attack drone with a range reported at around 1,000 kilometres, credited with many of the strikes on Russian oil refineries, depots and airfields from 2024. It sits at the heavy end of a family of Ukrainian long-range drones that also includes the Bober and UJ-22.

equipment.name: FP-1
equipment.role: Mass-produced long-range attack drone
equipment.description: A cheaper long-range attack drone from the Ukrainian firm Fire Point, shown publicly in 2025 with a stated production rate of over a hundred a day and a range of several hundred kilometres. It gives Ukraine a Shahed-like weapon for the campaign against Russian energy and logistics.
equipment.numbers: Fire Point stated production of around 100 a day in 2025; unverified.

equipment.name: Palianytsia and Peklo
equipment.role: Jet-powered drone-missiles
equipment.description: Ukraine's jet-powered 'missile-drones', announced in 2024, sit between a cruise missile and an attack drone: cheaper than a missile, faster than a Shahed. Palianytsia and the later Peklo were presented as strike weapons against airfields and depots within several hundred kilometres.

equipment.name: Interceptor drones (Ukraine)
equipment.role: Cheap drones that ram Shaheds and reconnaissance drones
equipment.description: Fast quadcopters and fixed-wing interceptors built to fly into Shahed drones, Orlans and Zalas at a fraction of the cost of a missile. Ukraine announced large purchases and production targets in 2025 as Shahed waves grew, with claims of hundreds of interceptions a night on the busiest nights.
equipment.numbers: Ukraine stated goals of 1,000 interceptor drones a day in 2025; unverified.

equipment.name: Interceptor drones (Russia)
equipment.role: Drones that hunt Ukrainian reconnaissance and long-range drones
equipment.description: Russia has fielded its own interceptor drones against Ukrainian reconnaissance types and the long-range drones flying at its refineries, alongside conventional air defence and helicopters used as drone hunters.

equipment.name: MAGURA V5
equipment.role: Uncrewed surface vessel that drove the Black Sea Fleet from Sevastopol
equipment.description: A Ukrainian naval drone from Defence Intelligence's programme, credited with sinking or damaging Russian warships and landing craft in 2023 and 2024 and, fitted with air-to-air missiles, with shooting down helicopters and even jets in 2025. Together with the Sea Baby it made Sevastopol unsafe for the fleet.

equipment.name: Sea Baby
equipment.role: Security Service naval drone used against the Crimean Bridge
equipment.description: The SBU's naval drone, used in the July 2023 attack on the Crimean Bridge and against ships and ports. Later versions carried rocket launchers and launched FPV drones from the sea.

equipment.name: Ground robots (Ukraine)
equipment.role: Tracked and wheeled robots for logistics, mining and casualty evacuation
equipment.description: From 2024 Ukraine issued growing numbers of small ground robots that carry supplies, lay mines and evacuate the wounded along drone-watched routes where a human on foot is likely to be hit. Some carry machine guns or explosive charges.

equipment.name: Starlink
equipment.role: Satellite internet that carries Ukrainian battlefield communications
equipment.description: SpaceX's low-orbit constellation has carried much of Ukraine's tactical communications, drone video and command traffic since 2022, with tens of thousands of terminals paid for by allies. Its availability has been a political question, and Russia has obtained terminals through third countries despite restrictions.
equipment.numbers: Ukraine reported over 40,000 terminals in use by 2024.

equipment.name: Starlink (illicit Russian use)
equipment.role: Terminals bought abroad and used by Russian units
equipment.description: Ukrainian intelligence and journalists reported from 2024 that Russian units were using Starlink terminals bought through intermediaries, giving them the same fast links for drone control. SpaceX said it does not sell to Russia and has disabled terminals it identifies.

equipment.name: R-187P1 Azart
equipment.role: Russian encrypted tactical radio
equipment.description: Russia's main modern handheld tactical radio, meant to give encrypted frequency-hopping links to small units. Its patchy issue in 2022 left many Russian units on unencrypted radios and phones that Ukraine intercepted, a failure widely reported in the first year.

equipment.name: L3Harris and Motorola radios
equipment.role: Western encrypted radios in Ukrainian service
equipment.description: Ukraine's units rely on donated and purchased Western radios, including L3Harris Falcon sets and Motorola handhelds, alongside domestic Ukrainian radios, with Starlink for data. The mixture has made interoperability a persistent problem between brigades.

equipment.name: Delta and Kropyva
equipment.role: Battle management software that fuses drone feeds and reports
equipment.description: Delta is Ukraine's cloud-based situational awareness system, fed by drone video, reports and allied intelligence, adopted across the armed forces in 2023 and made NATO-compatible. Kropyva is the older artillery tablet application used by gun crews. Together they turned reconnaissance into fire missions in minutes.

equipment.name: Command systems (Russia)
equipment.role: Automated command and reconnaissance-strike networks
equipment.description: Russia entered the war with a patchy automated command system and has since built reconnaissance-strike loops around drone video, Telegram-based reporting and dedicated targeting software for Lancet and artillery units. Public detail is thin; assessments describe faster but still centralised targeting.

equipment.name: Krasukha-4
equipment.role: Ground-based jammer against radars and satellites
equipment.description: A truck-mounted broadband jammer meant to blind airborne radars and reconnaissance satellites over hundreds of kilometres. A Krasukha-4 command post was captured intact near Kyiv in March 2022, and the system has appeared in loss lists since.

equipment.name: R-330Zh Zhitel
equipment.role: Jammer against satellite navigation and mobile phones
equipment.description: A mobile jamming station against satellite phones, mobile networks and GNSS receivers, one of the systems behind the dense electronic warfare that forces both sides towards fibre-optic drones and inertial navigation.

equipment.name: Bukovel-AD and trench jammers
equipment.role: Anti-drone electronic warfare from vehicle to backpack scale
equipment.description: Ukraine fields the Bukovel-AD system against reconnaissance drones and a mass of smaller 'trench' jammers fitted to vehicles and carried by infantry to break FPV control links. Their effectiveness fell as both sides moved to new frequencies and fibre-optic control.

equipment.name: Pole-21
equipment.role: GNSS jamming network mounted on cell towers
equipment.description: A jamming system installed on mobile-phone masts to deny GPS, GLONASS and Galileo over wide areas, used to protect Russian cities and rear areas from guided munitions and drones. Its interference is visible in the GPS interference map under the Cyber control.

equipment.name: Jam-resistant navigation (Ukraine)
equipment.role: Anti-jam antennas and inertial navigation for drones and munitions
equipment.description: Ukrainian long-range drones and Western guided munitions increasingly carry controlled reception pattern antennas, inertial units and terrain-matching to fly through jamming. Reported HIMARS and JDAM accuracy problems in 2023 drove the change.

equipment.name: S-400 Triumf
equipment.role: Long-range surface-to-air missile system
equipment.description: Russia's premier long-range air defence system, also used to fire ballistic-trajectory missiles at Ukrainian cities. S-400 batteries in Crimea and occupied territory have been struck repeatedly by ATACMS, Storm Shadow and drones, with radars and launchers documented destroyed.

equipment.name: S-300V4 and S-300PM
equipment.role: Army and air-force long-range air defence
equipment.description: Older long-range systems that remain widespread; the S-300V4 is the army's version with anti-ballistic missiles, and S-300P variants have been fired at ground targets in Kharkiv and Zaporizhzhia. Their radars are a favoured target for HIMARS and Ukrainian drones.

equipment.name: MIM-104 Patriot
equipment.role: The only Ukrainian system that reliably intercepts ballistic missiles
equipment.description: Patriot batteries arrived in April 2023 and shot down Kinzhal and Iskander missiles over Kyiv within weeks. They are the backbone of ballistic-missile defence for the capital and other cities, and interceptor supply, not launchers, has been the recurring limit, with each PAC-3 missile costing millions of dollars.
equipment.numbers: Ukraine has been reported to operate several batteries; exact numbers and interceptor stocks are not public.

equipment.name: SAMP/T
equipment.role: European long-range system with Aster missiles
equipment.description: The Franco-Italian SAMP/T, delivered from 2023, gives Ukraine a second long-range system able to engage ballistic missiles, with Aster 30 interceptors. Missile supply has been limited.

equipment.name: Buk-M2 and Buk-M3
equipment.role: Tracked medium-range air defence with the ground forces
equipment.description: The Buk family provides medium-range cover for Russian ground formations and has been fired at aircraft, HIMARS rockets and drones. Ukraine also fields older Buk-M1s, some adapted to fire Western Sea Sparrow missiles under the FrankenSAM programme.

equipment.name: NASAMS
equipment.role: Medium-range system firing AMRAAM missiles
equipment.description: NASAMS arrived in November 2022 and has been credited with high interception rates against cruise missiles and drones around Kyiv and other cities. It fires the same AMRAAM missiles as Western fighters, which eases supply but competes with F-16 stocks.

equipment.name: IRIS-T SLM
equipment.role: German medium-range system, Ukraine was its first user
equipment.description: Ukraine received the first IRIS-T SLM battery in October 2022, before Germany's own forces, and has reported very high hit rates against cruise missiles and Shaheds. Germany has committed further batteries and short-range SLS launchers.

equipment.name: MIM-23 Hawk
equipment.role: Cold War medium-range system returned to service
equipment.description: Refurbished Hawk batteries from Spain and US stocks gave Ukraine additional medium-range cover from 2023, valued for plentiful missiles against Shahed waves rather than for the newest threats.

equipment.name: Pantsir-S1
equipment.role: Gun and missile point defence for bases and cities
equipment.description: A truck-mounted system with two guns and short-range missiles that guards Russian airfields, the Kremlin and oil facilities against drones. It has been both a frequent Ukrainian target and a frequent claimant of drone kills; footage of Pantsirs on Moscow rooftops became a symbol of the drone campaign.

equipment.name: Tor-M2
equipment.role: Tracked short-range system against drones and rockets
equipment.description: A tracked short-range air defence system moving with Russian brigades, often credited in Russian reporting with shooting down Ukrainian drones and HIMARS rockets, and often found in Ukrainian strike footage.

equipment.name: Flakpanzer Gepard
equipment.role: Twin 35 mm anti-aircraft tank, the best Shahed killer per shot
equipment.description: Retired German anti-aircraft tanks supplied from 2022 became one of Ukraine's most cost-effective defences against Shahed drones, each kill costing a burst of 35 mm shells rather than a missile. Ammunition supply was solved by Rheinmetall restarting production.
equipment.numbers: Germany and the United States supplied several dozen Gepards.

equipment.name: Skynex and Skyranger
equipment.role: Modern 35 mm gun systems with airburst ammunition
equipment.description: Rheinmetall's Skynex gun system and vehicle-mounted Skyranger turrets bring programmable airburst ammunition against drones, supplied in small numbers from 2023 and 2024 to defend cities and infrastructure.

equipment.name: Igla and Verba MANPADS
equipment.role: Shoulder-launched missiles against helicopters and drones
equipment.description: Russian infantry carries Igla-S and the newer Verba shoulder-launched missiles, which have downed Ukrainian helicopters and attack jets flying low near the line. Both sides also mount MANPADS on vehicles as improvised air defence.

equipment.name: Stinger, Piorun and mobile fire groups
equipment.role: MANPADS and pickup-mounted machine guns against drones
equipment.description: Western shoulder-launched missiles were decisive against Russian helicopters in 2022. Against Shahed waves Ukraine relies on hundreds of mobile fire groups: pickups with heavy machine guns, searchlights and thermal sights that shoot drones down cheaply along their approach routes.

equipment.name: Counter-drone layers (Ukraine)
equipment.role: Acoustic sensors, jammers, interceptors and guns in depth
equipment.description: Ukraine's defence against Shaheds is a layered system: thousands of acoustic sensors that track drones by sound, jammers, interceptor drones, mobile fire groups, gun systems and, as a last resort, missiles. Layering keeps the cost per kill far below the cost of a missile.

equipment.name: Counter-drone measures (Russia)
equipment.role: Cage armour, jammers, nets and drone hunters
equipment.description: Russian vehicles carry welded 'cope cages', anti-drone screens and jammers against FPVs; rear areas rely on Pantsir, helicopters and interceptor drones against Ukraine's long-range types. Netting over roads and 'turtle tank' improvisations show how far the FPV threat has changed the battlefield.

equipment.name: 9K720 Iskander-M
equipment.role: Short-range ballistic missile, Russia's most accurate strike weapon
equipment.description: A road-mobile ballistic missile with a range of about 500 kilometres and a manoeuvring warhead that only Patriot has reliably intercepted. Used throughout the war against cities, command posts and airfields, often paired with the Iskander-K cruise missile from the same launcher.
equipment.numbers: The General Staff's cumulative claim for missile launchers is shown in the figures above.

equipment.name: Kh-47M2 Kinzhal
equipment.role: Air-launched ballistic missile fired from MiG-31s
equipment.description: An Iskander derivative launched from MiG-31K interceptors, presented by Russia as an unstoppable hypersonic weapon until Patriot crews shot several down over Kyiv in May 2023. It remains among the hardest missiles to intercept.

equipment.name: KN-23 (North Korean)
equipment.role: North Korean ballistic missiles supplied to Russia
equipment.description: From late 2023 Russia fired North Korean KN-23 and KN-24 ballistic missiles at Ukrainian cities, confirmed by debris analysis. Early examples were inaccurate; Ukrainian intelligence later reported improved accuracy as North Korea gained battlefield data.

equipment.name: Oreshnik
equipment.role: Intermediate-range ballistic missile first fired at Dnipro in November 2024
equipment.description: An intermediate-range ballistic missile with multiple warheads, fired at Dnipro on 21 November 2024 in what Russia called a test after Ukraine's first ATACMS strikes on Russian territory. Its inert warheads did limited damage; the launch was a signal rather than a battlefield weapon, and Russia announced deployment to Belarus.

equipment.name: MGM-140 ATACMS
equipment.role: HIMARS-launched ballistic missile out to 300 kilometres
equipment.description: ATACMS arrived secretly in October 2023 and destroyed helicopters at Berdiansk and Luhansk on their first use; the 300-kilometre version followed in 2024 and hit airfields and air defence in Crimea. Permission to fire into Russia came in November 2024 and drew the Oreshnik launch in reply.

equipment.name: Kh-101 and Kh-555
equipment.role: Air-launched cruise missiles fired from Tu-95 and Tu-160 bombers
equipment.description: The main long-range cruise missiles of the strategic bombers, launched from over Russia at power stations and cities in the recurring winter campaigns. Production continued through sanctions with imported electronics, and later missiles added decoys and larger warheads.
equipment.numbers: The General Staff's cumulative cruise missile claim is shown in the figures above.

equipment.name: 3M-14 Kalibr
equipment.role: Ship- and submarine-launched cruise missile from the Black Sea and Caspian
equipment.description: Fired from Black Sea Fleet corvettes, frigates and Kilo-class submarines, Kalibr salvoes opened many of the mass strikes. Ukrainian naval drones and missile strikes pushed the launch platforms out of Sevastopol and reduced the number of launches from the sea.

equipment.name: Kh-22 and Kh-32
equipment.role: Heavy anti-ship missiles fired at cities from Tu-22M3 bombers
equipment.description: Soviet-era supersonic anti-ship missiles with warheads near a tonne, fired at land targets with poor accuracy; a Kh-22 destroyed the Kremenchuk shopping centre in June 2022 and an apartment block in Dnipro in January 2023. Ukraine had no interceptor for them until Patriot.

equipment.name: 3M22 Zircon
equipment.role: Hypersonic cruise missile used in small numbers
equipment.description: Russia's hypersonic anti-ship cruise missile, fired at Kyiv from early 2024 in small numbers and confirmed from debris. Its speed makes it hard to intercept, but numbers have been low.

equipment.name: Storm Shadow / SCALP-EG
equipment.role: Air-launched cruise missile carried by Su-24s
equipment.description: Supplied from May 2023 and carried by adapted Su-24M bombers, Storm Shadow and its French twin destroyed the Black Sea Fleet headquarters in Sevastopol and a submarine in dry dock. Permission to fire into Russia followed in November 2024.

equipment.name: R-360 Neptune
equipment.role: Domestic cruise missile that sank the Moskva, later a land-attack weapon
equipment.description: Ukraine's anti-ship cruise missile sank the cruiser Moskva in April 2022. A land-attack version with longer range followed and has been used against targets in Crimea and Russia; Ukraine announced a 'Long Neptune' with a range of around 1,000 kilometres in 2025.

equipment.name: FP-5 Flamingo
equipment.role: Heavy long-range cruise missile shown in 2025
equipment.description: A large ground-launched cruise missile from Fire Point, presented in August 2025 with a stated warhead over a tonne and range of about 3,000 kilometres. Ukraine reported its first combat uses against targets in Russia later that year; independent confirmation of numbers is limited.
equipment.numbers: Fire Point stated a target of several missiles a day; unverified.

equipment.name: M142 HIMARS and GMLRS
equipment.role: Guided rocket artillery that changed the war in summer 2022
equipment.description: HIMARS launchers firing GPS-guided GMLRS rockets to about 80 kilometres arrived in June 2022 and destroyed Russian ammunition depots, bridges and command posts, forcing the withdrawal from Kherson. Russian jamming later degraded accuracy until updated guidance restored it.
equipment.numbers: The United States and allies supplied several dozen HIMARS and M270 launchers.

equipment.name: Tornado-S
equipment.role: Guided 300 mm rocket artillery
equipment.description: The modernised Smerch with satellite-guided 300 mm rockets, Russia's answer to HIMARS for strikes on airfields and depots at up to 120 kilometres.

equipment.name: UMPK glide bombs (FAB-500 to FAB-3000)
equipment.role: Cheap wing kits that turned dumb bombs into stand-off weapons
equipment.description: From early 2023 Russian Su-34s dropped Soviet-era FAB bombs fitted with folding wings and satellite guidance from outside the range of most Ukrainian air defence, up to a hundred a day by 2024. They levelled defensive positions at Avdiivka and Vuhledar and drove the pressure for F-16s and longer-range air defence.
equipment.numbers: Ukrainian officials reported several thousand glide bombs a month at the 2024 peak.

equipment.name: JDAM-ER and GLSDB
equipment.role: Western glide bombs and ground-launched small diameter bombs
equipment.description: Ukraine received JDAM-ER guided glide bombs for its MiG-29s and later F-16s, and the ground-launched GLSDB fired from HIMARS. Both suffered from Russian GPS jamming in 2023 and 2024 before updated guidance improved results.

equipment.name: 2S19 Msta-S
equipment.role: 152 mm self-propelled howitzer, the backbone of Russian artillery
equipment.description: Russia's standard tracked 152 mm howitzer, firing conventional and Krasnopol laser-guided shells. Russian artillery fired far more shells than Ukraine through 2022 and 2023, sustained by domestic production and North Korean supply, while losing hundreds of guns to counter-battery fire and Lancets.
equipment.numbers: The General Staff's cumulative artillery claim is shown in the figures above; Oryx documents around two thousand Russian artillery losses.

equipment.name: 2S7 Pion and Malka
equipment.role: 203 mm heavy guns for long-range fire
equipment.description: Soviet 203 mm guns brought out of storage for the long-range fire that reduced Bakhmut and Avdiivka. Ukraine also fields the 2S7 and once captured a number of them.

equipment.name: M1989 Koksan (North Korean)
equipment.role: 170 mm North Korean guns delivered to Russia
equipment.description: North Korea supplied its 170 mm Koksan self-propelled guns to Russia from late 2024, seen on Russian railways and later on the front, along with millions of shells that helped sustain Russian fire.

equipment.name: 2S22 Bohdana
equipment.role: Ukrainian-built 155 mm wheeled howitzer
equipment.description: Ukraine's own NATO-calibre howitzer, first used at Snake Island in 2022 and produced at a rate reported above twenty a month by 2024 and 2025, making it the most numerous new gun in the army. It fires the same 155 mm ammunition as Western donations.
equipment.numbers: Ukraine reported production of 20 or more a month in 2024 and 2025.

equipment.name: CAESAR, PzH 2000, Krab, Archer
equipment.role: Western 155 mm self-propelled howitzers
equipment.description: Ukraine's Western self-propelled guns range from the truck-mounted CAESAR and Archer, valued for shoot-and-scoot against counter-battery fire, to the tracked PzH 2000 and Polish Krab. Barrel wear and maintenance have been recurring issues at wartime firing rates.

equipment.name: M777 howitzer
equipment.role: Towed 155 mm howitzer, the first Western gun in numbers
equipment.description: Nearly two hundred M777s arrived in spring 2022 and fired the Excalibur guided shell; their light weight helped mobility but made them vulnerable to Lancets, and many have been damaged and repaired.
equipment.numbers: Around 190 were supplied in 2022.

equipment.name: D-30, Msta-B and Giatsint-B
equipment.role: Towed Soviet-era guns drawn from deep storage
equipment.description: As self-propelled guns were lost, Russia pulled towed 122 mm and 152 mm guns from Soviet storage sites, visible in satellite counts of shrinking depots. Both sides also use towed guns with the many mobilised units.

equipment.name: BM-21 Grad and Tornado-G
equipment.role: 122 mm multiple rocket launchers
equipment.description: The truck-mounted Grad and its modernised Tornado-G version deliver area fire on Ukrainian positions and towns, the most numerous rocket launchers on both sides. Ukraine fields Grads too, with domestic rockets and Czech RM-70 variants.
equipment.numbers: The General Staff's cumulative rocket launcher claim is shown in the figures above.

equipment.name: M270 MLRS and MARS II
equipment.role: Tracked launchers firing the same GMLRS rockets as HIMARS
equipment.description: The tracked M270 family from the UK, Germany and France doubled Ukraine's guided rocket capacity in 2022 alongside HIMARS.

equipment.name: TOS-1A Solntsepyok and TOS-2
equipment.role: Thermobaric rocket launchers on a tank chassis
equipment.description: Short-range launchers firing thermobaric rockets that devastate trenches and buildings, used at Mariupol, Bakhmut and Vuhledar. Their short range puts them within reach of drones, and dozens have been documented destroyed.

equipment.name: AK-12 and AK-74M
equipment.role: Standard 5.45 mm rifles
equipment.description: The AK-74M remains the most common Russian rifle, with the newer AK-12 issued from 2018 and revised during the war after complaints about its selector and rail. Mobilised troops have also been seen with older AKMs from storage.

equipment.name: AK-74, Fort-221 and Western rifles
equipment.role: A mixed inventory of 5.45 mm and 5.56 mm rifles
equipment.description: Most Ukrainian infantry still carry the AK-74 in 5.45 mm, with the Israeli-designed Fort-221 in special units and growing numbers of Western 5.56 mm rifles such as the M4, FN SCAR and Czech CZ Bren 2 from donations. The two calibres complicate supply.

equipment.name: PKM, PKP Pecheneg and Kord
equipment.role: General-purpose and heavy machine guns
equipment.description: The 7.62 mm PK family and the 12.7 mm Kord are found in every Russian platoon and on vehicles; the Kord and older NSV serve as improvised anti-drone guns on trucks.

equipment.name: M240, M2 Browning and Soviet types
equipment.role: Machine guns including the drone-hunting M2
equipment.description: Ukraine uses donated M240s and M2 Brownings alongside PKMs and DShKs; the M2 with a thermal sight is the standard weapon of the mobile fire groups that hunt Shahed drones at night.

equipment.name: Javelin, NLAW and Stugna-P
equipment.role: The anti-tank weapons that broke the 2022 armoured columns
equipment.description: Javelin and NLAW became symbols of the defence of Kyiv, and Ukraine's own Stugna-P laser-guided missile has a long record of tank kills. As FPV drones took over the anti-armour role, these weapons became a second layer rather than the first.
equipment.numbers: The United States announced over 10,000 Javelins by 2023; the UK supplied several thousand NLAWs.

equipment.name: RPG-7, RPG-30 and Kornet
equipment.role: Rocket-propelled grenades and the Kornet guided missile
equipment.description: Russian infantry carries the RPG-7 and disposable RPG-26 and RPG-30 launchers; the Kornet anti-tank missile, also mounted on vehicles, has killed Western tanks including Leopard 2s and Abrams. RPG warheads are also the most common FPV drone payload.

equipment.name: 2B14 Podnos and 2S12 Sani mortars
equipment.role: 82 mm and 120 mm mortars
equipment.description: Mortars provide the closest fire support on both sides; Russia's 82 mm Podnos and 120 mm Sani, and Ukraine's equivalents plus Western 60 mm and 120 mm mortars, fire more rounds daily than most people expect.

equipment.name: Mk 19 and UAG-40 grenade launchers
equipment.role: Automatic grenade launchers for trench fighting
equipment.description: Automatic grenade launchers, American Mk 19s and Ukrainian UAG-40s, sit in Ukrainian defensive positions alongside Soviet AGS-17s; the same 40 mm and 30 mm grenades are dropped from drones.

equipment.name: T-90M Proryv
equipment.role: Russia's most modern tank in production
equipment.description: The T-90M is Russia's best tank in quantity, with new armour, sights and a remote machine gun, and the type Uralvagonzavod concentrates on. Many have been lost, several captured intact by Ukraine, and most now carry improvised cages and screens against drones.
equipment.numbers: Oryx documents over a hundred T-90M losses; the General Staff's cumulative tank claim is shown in the figures above.

equipment.name: T-72B3 and T-80BVM
equipment.role: The most numerous Russian tanks
equipment.description: Modernised T-72s and gas-turbine T-80s make up the bulk of Russian tank losses and of the tanks still in service. Refurbishment of stored hulls, rather than new production, has sustained the numbers, and satellite counts show storage yards emptying.
equipment.numbers: Oryx documents several thousand Russian tank losses of all types.

equipment.name: T-62 and T-55
equipment.role: Cold War tanks pulled from storage
equipment.description: From 2022 Russia reactivated T-62s and even T-55s to replace losses, using them as assault guns and fire support with mobilised units. Their appearance became a measure of how deeply reserves were being drawn down.

equipment.name: T-64BV and T-64BM Bulat
equipment.role: Ukraine's standard tank, built in Kharkiv
equipment.description: The T-64 has been Ukraine's main tank since independence, kept running by the Kharkiv plant that built it. Ukraine also fields captured Russian T-72s and T-80s in numbers that at times exceeded its Western deliveries.

equipment.name: Leopard 2A4, 2A6 and Strv 122
equipment.role: Western tanks delivered from 2023
equipment.description: European Leopard 2s arrived for the 2023 counteroffensive and took losses in the minefields of Zaporizhzhia; they remain Ukraine's most capable tanks, with the 2A6 and Swedish Strv 122 the best protected. Spare parts and repair capacity have limited availability.
equipment.numbers: Around 100 Leopard 2s and 100 older Leopard 1A5s were pledged.

equipment.name: M1A1 Abrams and Challenger 2
equipment.role: American and British tanks in small numbers
equipment.description: The United States supplied 31 M1A1 Abrams and the UK 14 Challenger 2s. Both proved vulnerable to drones and mines in the Avdiivka fighting and were pulled back from the front for a period in 2024; Australia later pledged additional Abrams.
equipment.numbers: 31 Abrams and 14 Challenger 2s delivered by 2024.

equipment.name: BMP-3 and BMP-2
equipment.role: Tracked infantry fighting vehicles
equipment.description: The BMP-2 is the most common Russian infantry vehicle and the BMP-3 the most modern in production, both losing thin-armoured hulls in large numbers to mines, artillery and FPVs. Losses of infantry vehicles exceed tank losses several times over.
equipment.numbers: The General Staff's cumulative armoured vehicle claim is shown in the figures above.

equipment.name: M2A2 Bradley
equipment.role: Well-armoured American infantry fighting vehicle
equipment.description: The Bradley became one of Ukraine's most valued vehicles for its protection and its 25 mm gun, with crews surviving hits that would have destroyed a BMP. Losses in the 2023 counteroffensive were often repairable, and a Bradley famously defeated a T-90M near Stepove in January 2024.
equipment.numbers: More than 300 were supplied by the United States.

equipment.name: CV90 and Marder 1A3
equipment.role: European infantry fighting vehicles
equipment.description: Sweden's CV90 and Germany's Marder gave Ukrainian mechanised brigades modern vehicles from 2023, and Ukraine agreed to produce CV90s domestically. Marders also serve as drone-defence and evacuation vehicles.

equipment.name: BTR-82A and MT-LB
equipment.role: Wheeled and tracked armoured personnel carriers
equipment.description: The BTR-82A wheeled carrier and the MT-LB tractor carry Russian infantry and have been lost by the thousand; the MT-LB has also been fitted with naval guns and rocket pods as improvised fire support, a sign of shortages.

equipment.name: M113, Stryker and BTR-4
equipment.role: Armoured personnel carriers including Ukraine's own BTR-4
equipment.description: Hundreds of M113s from a dozen countries carry Ukrainian infantry and the wounded; Strykers arrived in 2023, and the Ukrainian-built BTR-4 with a 30 mm gun continues in production at Kharkiv.

equipment.name: MaxxPro, Bushmaster, Kozak and Novator
equipment.role: Mine-protected vehicles for infantry and evacuation
equipment.description: Mine-resistant trucks from US and Australian stocks, and Ukrainian-built Kozak and Novator vehicles, carry infantry to the line where tracked vehicles draw too much fire. They are among the most common vehicles in drone footage from both sides.

equipment.name: Tigr, Typhoon and motorcycles
equipment.role: Light protected vehicles and, increasingly, unprotected transport
equipment.description: Russia's Tigr and Typhoon protected vehicles have been joined since 2024 by motorcycles, quad bikes, golf carts and civilian cars for assaults, because drones make any vehicle a target and small numbers of fast riders sometimes get through.

equipment.name: Su-35S and Su-30SM
equipment.role: Air-superiority fighters that keep Ukrainian jets back
equipment.description: Russia's modern fighters patrol from inside Russian airspace with long-range R-37M missiles, denying Ukrainian aircraft the front line. Losses have been modest compared with ground attack types, and Ukraine's Patriot ambushes have caught several near the border.

equipment.name: F-16 Fighting Falcon
equipment.role: Ukraine's first Western fighters, flying from August 2024
equipment.description: European F-16s began operations in August 2024, mostly shooting down cruise missiles and drones and later dropping guided bombs. Pilot training and airfield vulnerability limit their use, and several have been lost, including to friendly fire and Russian missiles.
equipment.numbers: Around 85 were pledged by four countries.

equipment.name: Mirage 2000-5F and MiG-29
equipment.role: French fighters delivered in 2025 beside the Soviet-era fleet
equipment.description: France delivered Mirage 2000-5Fs in 2025 adapted for air defence and SCALP missiles. Ukraine's MiG-29s and Su-27s, reinforced from Poland and Slovakia, still fly most sorties with HARM anti-radar missiles and glide bombs.

equipment.name: Su-34
equipment.role: The bomber that drops most glide bombs
equipment.description: The Su-34 fighter-bomber carries the UMPK glide bombs that dominate Russian air support. Ukraine has shot down dozens with Patriot ambushes and destroyed others on airfields, but production continues.
equipment.numbers: Oryx documents several dozen Su-34 losses.

equipment.name: Su-25 and Su-24M
equipment.role: Ground-attack jets used at the front
equipment.description: Russian Su-25s fire unguided rockets in lofted attacks near the line and have suffered heavy losses to MANPADS; Ukraine's own Su-25s and Su-24Ms, the latter adapted to carry Storm Shadow, fly similar profiles.

equipment.name: Ka-52 and Mi-28
equipment.role: Attack helicopters with long-range anti-tank missiles
equipment.description: The Ka-52 was one of Russia's most effective weapons during the 2023 counteroffensive, firing Vikhr missiles from beyond MANPADS range at advancing Ukrainian columns. Ukraine's ATACMS strikes on Berdiansk and Luhansk in October 2023 destroyed a number on the ground.
equipment.numbers: Oryx documents over 60 Ka-52 losses.

equipment.name: Mi-8, Mi-24 and Black Hawk
equipment.role: Transport and attack helicopters
equipment.description: Ukraine's Mi-8s and Mi-24s fly resupply, evacuation and rocket attacks at low level, with Czech and Slovak donations and a small number of Western Black Hawks used for special operations.

equipment.name: Tu-95MS, Tu-160 and Tu-22M3
equipment.role: Strategic bombers that launch the cruise missile waves
equipment.description: The bombers launch Kh-101, Kh-555 and Kh-22 missiles from deep inside Russia. Ukraine's June 2025 Operation Spiderweb used smuggled FPV drones to hit bombers on airfields as far as Siberia, damaging or destroying a significant share of the small Tu-95 and Tu-22M3 fleets.
equipment.numbers: Ukraine claimed 41 aircraft hit in Operation Spiderweb; US officials assessed a lower number.

equipment.name: A-50 airborne early warning
equipment.role: Radar aircraft, two shot down in early 2024
equipment.description: Russia's A-50 radar aircraft direct fighters and air defence; Ukraine shot down two in January and February 2024 and damaged another at Machulishchy in Belarus in 2023, leaving Russia with a handful.

equipment.name: Black Sea Fleet surface ships
equipment.role: Frigates, corvettes and landing ships, many lost or withdrawn
equipment.description: The fleet lost its flagship Moskva in April 2022 and then landing ships, a submarine and patrol ships to missiles and naval drones, before withdrawing most vessels from Sevastopol to Novorossiysk in late 2023. Its remaining corvettes still launch Kalibr missiles from the eastern Black Sea.
equipment.numbers: Ukraine claims around a third of the fleet destroyed or disabled; Oryx documents over 20 vessels lost or damaged.

equipment.name: Improved Kilo-class submarines
equipment.role: Diesel submarines that launch Kalibr missiles
equipment.description: Six Improved Kilo submarines of the Black Sea Fleet launch Kalibr cruise missiles; one, Rostov-on-Don, was destroyed in dry dock by Storm Shadow in September 2023 and again after repair in August 2024.

equipment.name: Ukrainian Navy: Neptune batteries, patrol boats and marines
equipment.role: A navy without large ships that dominates the western Black Sea
equipment.description: Ukraine scuttled its flagship in 2022 and fights at sea with coastal Neptune missiles, naval drones, small patrol boats from the United States and Europe and marine brigades that hold the Dnipro's islands and banks. It reopened the grain corridor without a single warship.

forces.name: Supreme Commander-in-Chief
forces.role: The President of Russia commands the armed forces and, by reporting, intervenes in operational decisions down to brigade level.

forces.name: Ministry of Defence
forces.role: Political and industrial direction of the war: mobilisation, procurement and the wartime economy. Andrei Belousov, an economist, replaced Sergei Shoigu in May 2024.
forces.strength: Russia's declared armed forces ceiling rose to 1.5 million service personnel in 2024 (presidential decree); the deployed force in and around Ukraine is estimated by Ukrainian and Western officials at around 600,000 to 700,000.

forces.name: General Staff and Joint Grouping of Forces
forces.role: Chief of the General Staff Valery Gerasimov has commanded the Joint Grouping of Forces in Ukraine since January 2023, succeeding Sergei Surovikin; he was kept on past retirement age in 2025.

forces.name: Groupings of forces
forces.role: The front is divided into named groupings, each built on a military district headquarters and several combined-arms armies: North (Kharkiv and Sumy axes), West (Kupiansk and Lyman), South (Siversk and the Donetsk sector), Centre (Pokrovsk and the western Donetsk axis), East (Vuhledar and the Zaporizhzhia boundary) and Dnepr (Zaporizhzhia and Kherson).

forces.name: Grouping North
forces.role: Formed in 2024 from the Leningrad Military District's forces for the Kharkiv incursion in May 2024, then the defence of Kursk and the Sumy border. Includes the 6th and 11th Armies and the 44th Army Corps.

forces.name: Grouping West
forces.role: Built on the 1st Guards Tank Army and 20th Combined Arms Army, fighting on the Kupiansk, Lyman and Borova axes in Kharkiv and Luhansk oblasts.

forces.name: Grouping Centre
forces.role: The Central Military District's forces, including the 2nd and 41st Combined Arms Armies and later the 51st Army (the former 1st Donetsk Corps), which carried the main effort against Avdiivka in 2024 and Pokrovsk in 2024 and 2025.

forces.name: Grouping South
forces.role: The Southern Military District's 8th Combined Arms Army with the 3rd Army Corps and the former Luhansk corps, responsible for Bakhmut, Chasiv Yar, Toretsk and Siversk.

forces.name: Grouping East
forces.role: Eastern Military District forces, the 5th, 29th, 35th and 36th Armies, on the Vuhledar and Velyka Novosilka axes at the boundary of Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia oblasts.

forces.name: Grouping Dnepr
forces.role: Holds the Zaporizhzhia front and the left bank of the Dnipro in Kherson with the 58th and 49th Armies and the 18th Army, facing the Ukrainian bridgeheads and the Orikhiv axis.

forces.name: Airborne Forces (VDV)
forces.role: The 7th, 76th, 98th and 106th divisions and separate brigades, used as the mobile reserve and in the heaviest fighting from Hostomel in 2022 to Kursk in 2024 and 2025. Losses have been heavy and units were rebuilt with mobilised soldiers.
forces.strength: Pre-war establishment around 45,000; expanded on paper with new regiments.

forces.name: Naval Infantry
forces.role: The 155th, 40th, 61st and 810th brigades of the fleets' naval infantry, converted to divisions on paper from 2024, fought at Mariupol, Vuhledar and Kursk with repeated heavy losses.

forces.name: Aerospace Forces (VKS)
forces.role: Fighters, Su-34 bombers, the Long-Range Aviation bombers that fire cruise missiles, and the air defence forces. Missile Troops and Artillery and the Iskander brigades sit with the ground forces.

forces.name: Black Sea Fleet
forces.role: Headquartered in Sevastopol until strikes and naval drones forced most ships to Novorossiysk; still launches Kalibr missiles and holds the Kerch Strait.

forces.name: Rosgvardia and Akhmat
forces.role: The National Guard occupies and polices captured territory and fields its own combat units; the Chechen Akhmat formations, formally within Rosgvardia, took Wagner's assault role in some sectors after 2023.

forces.name: Storm-Z and Storm-V penal units
forces.role: Assault units of recruited prisoners attached to regular formations, successors to Wagner's prison recruitment, used for costly infantry attacks along the Donetsk front.

forces.name: North Korean contingent
forces.role: Around 11,000 to 12,000 Korean People's Army troops deployed to Kursk Oblast from late 2024, engaged from November 2024 and reinforced in 2025; North Korea also supplies shells, missiles and guns. Numbers are South Korean, Ukrainian and US estimates.
forces.strength: South Korean intelligence estimated 11,000 deployed by early 2025 plus reinforcements; casualties in the thousands.

forces.name: Supreme Commander-in-Chief
forces.role: The President of Ukraine commands the armed forces through the Staff of the Supreme Commander-in-Chief.

forces.name: Ministry of Defence
forces.role: Procurement, mobilisation policy and the defence industry; the ministry changed hands several times during the war and its leadership was contested in the 2026 command crisis.
forces.strength: Ukraine's armed forces number around one million personnel of whom a few hundred thousand serve in combat units, by official statements; exact figures are not published.

forces.name: Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces
forces.role: Oleksandr Syrskyi replaced Valerii Zaluzhnyi in February 2024 and was himself replaced by Mykhailo Drapatyi in July 2026 amid a military leadership crisis (reported structure; confirm against current reporting).

forces.name: General Staff
forces.role: Plans operations and publishes the daily loss claims shown on this page; the Chief of the General Staff post changed hands with the 2024 and 2026 command changes.

forces.name: Ground Forces
forces.role: The largest service: mechanised, motorised, tank, artillery and territorial units. In 2025 brigades were grouped into around 18 army corps in a reform intended to fix the span of control of the earlier operational-tactical groups.

forces.name: Army corps (2025 reform)
forces.role: Corps formed around experienced brigades, including the 1st Azov Corps of the National Guard, the 3rd Army Corps built on the 3rd Assault Brigade, and corps built on the 12th, 53rd and other brigades, each holding a sector with attached artillery and drone units.

forces.name: Operational groupings
forces.role: Regional joint commands over the corps: the eastern grouping (Donetsk and Luhansk fronts, formerly Khortytsia), the southern grouping (Zaporizhzhia and Kherson, formerly Tavria and Dnipro), the Kursk grouping of 2024 and 2025, and the northern border groupings for Sumy and Kharkiv.

forces.name: Air Assault Forces
forces.role: Ukraine's elite light infantry brigades (25th, 79th, 80th, 82nd, 95th and others), used as the fire brigade of the front from Hostomel to Kursk.

forces.name: Unmanned Systems Forces
forces.role: A separate branch created in 2024 for drone units, with dedicated strike regiments such as Magyar's Birds and Achilles that publish confirmed hits; drones now account for the majority of claimed Russian equipment losses.

forces.name: Air Force
forces.role: Fighters (MiG-29, Su-27, F-16, Mirage 2000), Su-24 and Su-25 strike aircraft, and the anti-aircraft missile forces that operate Patriot, SAMP/T, NASAMS and IRIS-T; publishes the nightly interception figures.

forces.name: Navy and Marines
forces.role: Coastal missile batteries, naval drones, small boats and the marine corps brigades that fought at Mariupol and hold the Dnipro delta.

forces.name: Territorial Defence Forces
forces.role: Regional brigades raised in 2022 from volunteers, now fighting as regular infantry across the front; many have been rebuilt several times.

forces.name: Special Operations Forces
forces.role: Raiding, sabotage and long-range reconnaissance inside occupied territory and Russia, alongside Defence Intelligence's own units and naval drone crews.

forces.name: National Guard and Border Guard
forces.role: Interior ministry forces that fight as line units: the National Guard's 1st Azov Corps and other brigades, and the State Border Guard Service's assault units in Kharkiv and Sumy.

forces.name: Defence Intelligence (HUR)
forces.role: The military intelligence directorate runs naval drones, deep strikes and special units and is a frequent source of the claims in this page's updates; treat its statements as an interested party's.

phases.label: Background, 2014 to 2021
phases.summary: Russia seized Crimea and fostered the war in the Donbas after the Maidan revolution; eight years of trench war followed along a static line while Ukraine rebuilt its army.

phases.label: Full-scale invasion, February to April 2022
phases.summary: Russia attacked from the north, east and south. The drive on Kyiv failed within weeks and Russian forces withdrew from the north, leaving Bucha and Irpin behind them.

phases.label: Battle for the Donbas, April to August 2022
phases.summary: Russia concentrated on the east, took Mariupol, Sievierodonetsk and Lysychansk with massed artillery, and was slowed only when HIMARS reached Ukraine.

phases.label: Ukrainian counteroffensives, autumn 2022
phases.summary: Ukraine broke through at Kharkiv and forced the Russian withdrawal from Kherson, while Russia annexed four regions on paper and mobilised 300,000 men.

phases.label: Winter attrition and Bakhmut, late 2022 to mid 2023
phases.summary: Russia struck the power grid all winter and Wagner ground through Bakhmut at enormous cost while both sides prepared for the summer.

phases.label: The 2023 counteroffensive
phases.summary: Ukraine's Western-equipped brigades attacked into deep minefields in Zaporizhzhia and gained little; at sea, naval drones and missiles drove the Black Sea Fleet from Sevastopol.

phases.label: Avdiivka and attrition, 2024
phases.summary: With US aid stalled for months, Russia took Avdiivka with glide bombs and human waves, opened a new front at Kharkiv and ground westward towards Pokrovsk.

phases.label: Kursk and the long-range war, August 2024 to spring 2025
phases.summary: Ukraine invaded Kursk Oblast and held a salient for months against Russian and North Korean troops; deep strikes on refineries and airfields grew on both sides and Russia fired the Oreshnik.

phases.label: Talks, drones and the 2025 summer offensive
phases.summary: Russia's summer offensive made slow, costly gains around Pokrovsk and Kostiantynivka while Shahed waves reached record size; the United States pushed peace plans that Kyiv and Europe reworked and Moscow rejected.

The war continued into its fifth year with a slow Russian advance, a growing drone war on both sides, a command crisis in Kyiv in the summer and no ceasefire. Later events appear in the updates feed above.

events.title: Russia seizes Crimea
events.text: Unmarked Russian troops took control of the Crimean parliament and the peninsula within days of the Maidan revolution; a staged referendum and annexation followed in March. The seizure was the opening of the Russo-Ukrainian war.

events.title: War begins in the Donbas
events.text: Russian-backed armed groups seized towns in Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts; the fighting that followed, including Ilovaisk and Debaltseve, killed some 14,000 people before 2022 and froze into a trench line under the Minsk agreements.

events.title: MH17 shot down
events.text: A Buk missile from Russia's 53rd Anti-Aircraft Brigade destroyed Malaysia Airlines flight 17 over the Donbas, killing 298 people; a Dutch court convicted three men in absentia in 2022.

events.title: Russian build-up and demands
events.text: Russia massed some 190,000 troops on Ukraine's borders and in Belarus through late 2021 and demanded that NATO never admit Ukraine, while denying any plan to attack.

events.title: The full-scale invasion begins
events.text: Putin announced a 'special military operation' and missiles struck cities across Ukraine as columns crossed from Belarus, Russia and Crimea. Airborne troops seized Hostomel airfield near Kyiv and were thrown back within a day.

events.title: The battle for Kyiv is won
events.text: Russian columns stalled north of Kyiv under ambushes, Javelins, artillery and their own logistics failures; by the end of March Russia announced a withdrawal from the north.

events.title: Bucha and the northern withdrawal
events.text: Ukrainian forces re-entering Bucha, Irpin and Borodianka found hundreds of murdered civilians. The evidence ended early peace talks in Istanbul and hardened Western support.

events.title: The cruiser Moskva sinks
events.text: Two Ukrainian Neptune missiles hit the Black Sea Fleet flagship, which sank the next day, the largest warship lost in combat since 1982.

events.title: Mariupol falls after Azovstal
events.text: After nearly three months of siege and the destruction of most of the city, the last defenders at the Azovstal steelworks surrendered on orders from Kyiv. Tens of thousands of civilians are believed to have died.

events.title: HIMARS enters the war
events.text: American HIMARS launchers began destroying Russian ammunition depots and bridges up to 80 kilometres behind the line, ending the artillery advantage that had taken Sievierodonetsk and Lysychansk.

events.title: Kharkiv counteroffensive
events.text: Ukrainian forces broke through thin Russian lines east of Kharkiv, took Balakliia, Kupiansk and Izium in a week and recovered most of the oblast, the war's fastest advance.

events.title: Russia announces mobilisation
events.text: Putin ordered the call-up of 300,000 reservists, the first Russian mobilisation since 1945; hundreds of thousands of men left the country and the annexation of four oblasts was proclaimed nine days later.

events.title: The Crimean Bridge is hit
events.text: A truck bomb collapsed part of the road bridge to Crimea; Russia answered with the first mass missile strikes on Ukraine's energy system, opening the winter campaign against the grid.

events.title: Kherson liberated
events.text: Cut off by HIMARS strikes on the Dnipro bridges, Russian forces withdrew from the only regional capital they had captured; Ukrainian troops entered the city to crowds in the streets.

events.title: Winter strikes on the power grid
events.text: Waves of cruise missiles and Shahed drones through the winter of 2022 to 2023 left millions without power and heat, without breaking the grid or public support.

events.title: Western tanks pledged
events.text: Germany, the United States and European partners agreed to send Leopard 2, Abrams and Challenger 2 tanks after months of hesitation, followed by Patriot batteries and, in May, Storm Shadow missiles.

events.title: Bakhmut falls to Wagner
events.text: After ten months of the war's longest battle, Wagner's prisoner-recruited assault groups took the ruined city at a cost estimated in the tens of thousands of casualties on each side.

events.title: Kakhovka dam destroyed
events.text: The dam on the Dnipro collapsed while under Russian control, flooding towns downstream, killing dozens and draining the reservoir that cooled the Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant.

events.title: The 2023 counteroffensive begins
events.text: Ukraine's new brigades attacked towards Melitopol and Berdiansk into dense minefields covered by Ka-52 helicopters and Lancets; Robotyne was taken in August but no breakthrough followed.

events.title: Wagner mutiny
events.text: Yevgeny Prigozhin's Wagner columns seized Rostov-on-Don and drove towards Moscow before a deal halted them; Prigozhin died in a plane crash two months later.

events.title: Black Sea Fleet headquarters struck
events.text: Storm Shadow missiles destroyed the fleet headquarters in Sevastopol; with a submarine and landing ship hit in dry dock and naval drones stalking the harbour, most of the fleet moved to Novorossiysk.

events.title: First ATACMS strikes
events.text: Secretly delivered ATACMS missiles destroyed helicopters at Berdiansk and Luhansk airfields, and Ukraine's counteroffensive was acknowledged to have stalled by November.

events.title: Avdiivka falls
events.text: After four months of assault under glide bombs and with Ukrainian ammunition rationed while US aid was blocked in Congress, Ukraine withdrew from the fortress town it had held since 2014.

events.title: Zaluzhnyi replaced by Syrskyi
events.text: President Zelenskyy replaced the popular commander-in-chief Valerii Zaluzhnyi with Oleksandr Syrskyi after months of reported disputes over mobilisation and strategy.

events.title: US aid resumes
events.text: Congress passed a 61 billion dollar package after a six-month blockage; ammunition and the 300-kilometre ATACMS reached the front within weeks. Ukraine also lowered its mobilisation age to 25.

events.title: Russian incursion north of Kharkiv
events.text: Russia opened a new front towards Vovchansk and Lyptsi, drawing Ukrainian reserves; it was contained within weeks and led allies to permit strikes into Russia near the border.

events.title: F-16s arrive
events.text: The first European F-16s entered Ukrainian service, initially against cruise missiles and drones; one was lost with its pilot in the first weeks.

events.title: Ukraine invades Kursk Oblast
events.text: Ukrainian brigades crossed the border and took Sudzha and some 1,000 square kilometres in days, the first foreign occupation of Russian territory since 1945; the salient held until spring 2025.

events.title: North Korean troops enter combat
events.text: Some 11,000 North Korean soldiers deployed to Kursk engaged Ukrainian forces from early November, confirmed by Kyiv, Seoul and Washington; two were captured in January 2025.

events.title: Oreshnik fired at Dnipro
events.text: Days after Ukraine's first ATACMS and Storm Shadow strikes inside Russia, Russia fired an intermediate-range ballistic missile with inert warheads at Dnipro as a signal to the West.

events.title: Washington changes course
events.text: The new US administration opened direct talks with Moscow, clashed publicly with Zelenskyy in the Oval Office and briefly paused aid and intelligence; Ukraine accepted a 30-day ceasefire proposal in March that Russia declined.

events.title: Kursk salient largely lost
events.text: Russian and North Korean forces, using fibre-optic drones against Ukrainian supply routes, retook Sudzha in March and most of the salient by late April.

events.title: Operation Spiderweb
events.text: FPV drones smuggled into Russia in lorry roofs struck strategic bombers on airfields from Murmansk to Irkutsk; Ukraine claimed 41 aircraft hit, US officials fewer. The operation exposed the bomber fleet to drones for the first time.

events.title: Russia's summer offensive
events.text: Russian forces pushed on Pokrovsk, Kostiantynivka and into Sumy and Dnipropetrovsk oblasts through the summer with small infantry groups and motorcycles, gaining ground slowly at heavy cost without a breakthrough.

events.title: Campaign against Russian refineries
events.text: Ukrainian long-range drones hit a large share of Russia's major refineries repeatedly through 2025, cutting output and causing fuel shortages in Russian regions; Russia answered with record Shahed and missile waves on Ukraine's grid.

events.title: The 28-point plan
events.text: A US 28-point peace plan, read as close to Russian terms, prompted counter-drafts from Kyiv and European capitals; Moscow rejected the revised versions and fighting continued.

events.title: Four years of full-scale war
events.text: On the fourth anniversary Zelenskyy put Ukrainian military deaths at about 55,000 with many more missing, a figure independent trackers consider low; estimates of Russian dead from named-casualty counts run far higher. All such figures are contested.

events.title: Command crisis in Kyiv
events.text: Amid protests over the defence ministry and the conduct of the war, Zelenskyy replaced Oleksandr Syrskyi with Mykhailo Drapatyi as commander-in-chief in July 2026 (reported; see current updates for later changes).
